content_voiceover: This slide summarizes the endothelium's antithrombotic functions as three functional categories sitting atop a layer of endothelial cells. The antiplatelet category includes nitric oxide, CD39, and prostacyclin, all of which suppress platelet activation and aggregation. The anticoagulant category includes heparan sulfate, which potentiates antithrombin, thrombomodulin and the endothelial protein C receptor, which together activate protein C, and tissue factor pathway inhibitor, or TFPI, which blocks the extrinsic tenase complex. The profibrinolytic category includes tissue plasminogen activator and urokinase-type plasminogen activator, both of which promote clot breakdown. Together these three arms explain why intact, healthy endothelium is fundamentally anti-thrombotic, and why endothelial injury or dysfunction is a central trigger for pathologic thrombosis, echoing the vascular injury component of Virchow's triad.
keypoints: Antiplatelet arm: nitric oxide, CD39, prostacyclin
Anticoagulant arm: heparan sulfate, thrombomodulin, EPCR, TFPI
Healthy endothelium is intrinsically antithrombotic; injury triggers thrombosis
keypoint_voiceover: Group these by function: antiplatelet factors are nitric oxide, CD39, and prostacyclin; anticoagulant factors are heparan sulfate, thrombomodulin, EPCR, and TFPI; profibrinolytic factors are t-PA and u-PA. Intact endothelium is inherently antithrombotic, so injury to it is a key trigger for pathologic clotting.
